newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD calls on Waigel to withdraw tax bill.
newsitem.headline: German SPD calls on Waigel to withdraw tax bill.

text.p: Germany's Social Democratic (SPD) opposition, wielding an upper-house majority capable of halting government tax plans, called on Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Monday to withdraw his 1997 tax bill.

SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine, commenting before Waigel meets SPD leaders for tax talks in the evening, also demanded cuts in the burden on families and workers and repeated demands for a major tax reform to be passed in 1998.

Positions have hardened in the debate over Waigel's tax bill, the one part of a 70 billion mark austerity package intended to cut levies and boost job creation which the SPD-controlled Bundesrat can block.
"My party is ready to create more fairness in the tax system. A big cut in the burden on low-income groups is needed for 1998," Lafontaine said in a statement.
Waigel, battling to contain an overshoot in new borrowing this year, has warned of dire consequences if the tax bill does not pass.

The measure is a key component of Waigel's bid to knock state finances into shape for EU economic and monetary union next year -- when fitness will be judged under the Maastricht Treaty for taking part in the launch of the single currency in 1999.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) sister party have said a major tax reform can only go through in 1999 -- after elections due to be held in 1998.

A first round of talks on the tax bill a week ago made no progress, and signs of willingness to compromise looked scant on Monday, with both sides saying progress had been made only on changes to inheritance taxes.
The SPD says that increases in child benefits would go through automatically if it blocked the tax bill.

The government responds that wealth taxes -- which the constitutional court has ordered scrapped -- would disappear next year. Without the passage of the tax bill, the government says, regions would face a multi-billion mark financing gap.

Kohl's parliamentary party leader Wolfgang Schaeuble told Monday's Frankfurter Allegemeine Zeitung newspaper that he saw no signs of movement by the SPD on wealth tax, child benefits, the phasing out of the solidarity surcharge or corporation tax.
Schaeuble said that, if the SPD stuck to its position, the coalition would consider breaking up the bill and passing the parts which are not subject to Bundesrat approval.
